title: How To Put An End To Roughhousing
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles roughhousing as a persistently tricky classroom management problem, one that can linger even in classrooms with otherwise solid discipline because of how impulsive the behavior is. After emphasizing that consistent enforcement of the classroom management plan remains foundational, he introduces two supplemental strategies aimed at making the rule genuinely resonate. The first is modeling exactly what roughhousing looks like — since many students interpret rules like "keep your hands and feet to yourself" narrowly — by physically demonstrating the behavior the teacher has witnessed. The second, more time-intensive strategy is modeling that same behavior in the specific locations where it tends to occur, such as hallways or transition lines, which reframes the act as socially unacceptable rather than harmless fun. Linsin contrasts this approach with the common but less effective tactic of lecturing or dramatizing disappointment, arguing that action-based modeling creates a stronger, more lasting association than words alone.
points: Roughhousing can persist even in well-managed classrooms because the behavior is impulsive despite consistent consequences.
Consistent enforcement of the classroom management plan remains the foundational first step and does most of the work.
Modeling exactly what roughhousing looks like clarifies the rule for students who interpret it too narrowly.
Reenacting the behavior in the specific locations where it occurs — hallways, lines, transitions — strengthens the association that it is unacceptable.
Action-based modeling reframes roughhousing as silly and out of place more effectively than lecturing or raised voices.
quotes: It isn’t uncommon to have otherwise solid classroom management and still struggle to get students to stop wrestling, play-fighting, and the like.
Many students assume that 'keep your hands and feet to yourself' refers only to malicious intent, even if you say otherwise.
Modeling the exact roughhousing behavior you're witnessing, or have witnessed in the past, makes it real and clarifies the definition.
When you model the exact behavior your students are engaging in, and how you’ll enforce it, you’ll see far less of that behavior.
By modeling in the place or places where it occurs, it reframes the act of roughhousing from harmless fun to a stigma they don’t want to be part of.
But the trick is to bring the behavior into sharper focus. It’s to label roughhousing as silly, absurd, and unacceptable within a place of learning—not through your words, but through your actions.
Your students, in turn, will finally make the connection. And refrain from the behavior.
